<section class="content-band">
<p class="section-kicker">About</p>
<h2 class="section-title">I study local government organization and public goods.</h2>
<div class="grid-two">
<div>
<p class="section-lede">My work asks how the organization of local governments affects the provision of public goods and the growth of U.S. metropolitan areas. I am especially interested in cases where institutional boundaries look administrative on paper, but change the coordination problem faced by residents, firms, and public officials.</p>
<p class="section-lede">That makes local government a useful meeting point for economics, finance, political economy, urban policy, and public administration. The empirical question is practical: when should fragmented jurisdictions compete, and when does growth require coordination across the whole metro area?</p>

<section class="content-band tint">
<p class="section-kicker">Current Research</p>
<h2 class="section-title">Local government centralization and metropolitan growth.</h2>
<div class="grid-two">
<article class="paper-card">
<div class="paper-topline">
<span class="tag coral">Job market paper</span>
<span class="tag">Local public finance</span>
<span class="tag gold">Growth</span>
</div>
<div class="paper-body">
<h2>Coordination vs. Competition: Local Government Centralization and Metropolitan Growth</h2>
<p class="abstract">The paper estimates how centralization in local government affects population growth in U.S. metropolitan areas. It uses local government employment data and an IV strategy based on historical post office patterns around Rural Free Delivery to separate coordination from competition.</p>
<div class="paper-links">
<a href="_site/Projects/WIEDEMANN_MUNI_CENTRALIZATION_2026.pdf">Read the paper</a>
<a href="_site/Projects/projects.html">View research page</a>
</div>
</div>
</article>
<aside class="note-panel">
<h3>Paper details</h3>
<p><strong>Setting:</strong> U.S. metropolitan statistical areas.</p>
<p><strong>Approach:</strong> local government employment data and an IV strategy based on historical post office patterns around Rural Free Delivery.</p>
<p><strong>Question:</strong> whether centralized or decentralized local government structures better promote growth.</p>
</aside>
</div>
</section>
<section class="content-band">
<p class="section-kicker">Research Themes</p>
<h2 class="section-title">Research themes</h2>
<div class="grid-three">
<article class="feature-card">
<h3>Coordination</h3>
<p>When public goods spill across jurisdictional borders, fragmented governments can struggle to internalize metro-wide benefits.</p>
</article>
<article class="feature-card">
<h3>Competition</h3>
<p>Decentralized governments may discipline each other through resident and firm mobility, creating pressure for efficient provision.</p>
</article>
<article class="feature-card">
<h3>Mechanisms</h3>
<p>Employment, fiscal capacity, tax revenue, and firm location decisions help identify the channels behind observed growth effects.</p>
</article>
</div>
